significantly reduce the gap between simulated and real-world performance.

The study of jet physics in radio galaxies and blazars has significantly advanced 
in the past decade, with a strong foundation of observational evidence. Radio galaxies 
with low activity levels display a jet that propagates along the black hole's equatorial plane 
and is influenced by the surrounding environment, while those with high activity levels show 
evidence of a jet that is able to break free from its constraints and travel more freely. 
Blazars, with their jets pointing directly towards Earth, offer a unique opportunity to 
study jet dynamics, with certain sub-classes displaying evidence of jet interactions with 
their surroundings. By examining the properties of jet dynamics in these objects, we can 
gain a deeper understanding of black hole physics and the interplay between black holes and 
their host galaxies.

This research focuses on estimating time-inconsistent models through sieve methods, 
which involve creating an approximating model that most closely aligns with the true model 
by minimizing discrepancies in the utility and probability measures. 
We establish the asymptotic behavior of estimators obtained by this method, 
and introduce a hybrid sieve estimator that achieves optimal statistical efficiency. 
Furthermore, we propose an asymptotic sieve empirical likelihood estimator that enables 
hypothesis testing beyond traditional methods. Inference results are obtained through sieve estimators, 
and our approach is demonstrated through simulations and real-world data applications.

The widespread use of social media has led to an increase in the popularity of online platforms, transforming the way people interact and share their thoughts with one another. However, a growing concern on the internet involves the prevalence of offensive language, posing a potential threat to online communities. This research paper delves into the issue of identifying and categorizing toxic comments left by users on online platforms. A novel approach to detecting abusive language involves the incorporation of a neural network model that utilizes a combination of linguistic features and advanced learning techniques. Experimental findings demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms established benchmarks by achieving exceptional accuracy, with a 3.2% improvement in F1-measure score.

The study of functional brain connections, a key area in neuroscience research, has been approached in various ways, but existing methods have limitations in different domains. While diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) provides insights into white matter, it has its own set of problems. Functional imaging methods such as fMRI and MEG offer dynamic information, but with their own set of limitations. Given the complexity and variability of brain function, a single imaging technique may not be sufficient to capture its full complexity. Deep learning methods have been successful in analyzing imaging data, but they have not been used to a great extent in discovering brain connections. Our research aims to develop a data-driven approach to studying brain connections using a combination of deep learning and graph theory. We have created a framework that can analyze brain data from various sources, including structural and functional imaging techniques, and has been shown to be effective in identifying brain connections in healthy individuals and those with schizophrenia.

This paper explores the application of dissipativity theory from control theory to the analysis of first-order optimization methods. By employing this approach, we establish a general framework for assessing the efficiency and stability of optimization methods. Building on this framework, we provide a comprehensive analysis of Nesterov's boosted method, supported by both theoretical and numerical evidence. Our theoretical results demonstrate that Nesterov's boosted method satisfies a dissipative relationship, indicating that it is stable and efficient. Furthermore, we extend the analysis to the infinite-dimensional domain, where we derive a dual dissipativity relationship for Nesterov's boosted method in a broad, non-specific setting.

This research investigates the performance of the IMEX-RK framework when applied to hyperbolic systems with varying and spatially diverse source terms, demonstrating that it yields stable boundary conditions at a linearized level when certain conditions are met. Building upon this, we establish the requirements for and propose novel, consistent boundary conditions at the boundary of an explicit system interacting with an implicit system. These conditions are validated through rigorous theoretical analysis and verified through numerical case studies that accurately replicate theoretical predictions.

Thin silicon films are highly sought after for photovoltaic applications, but their absorption rates are hindered by the short wavelength due to the significant resistance in ultrathin layers, as well as surface and interface losses. To address this challenge, researchers have employed a 1D and 2D photonic band gap back reflectors in simulations modeling a 100 nm silicon film, with a 1.5 eV direct bandgap, but only achieving 60% of the absorption achieved by a perfect absorber. Despite this limitation, the 2D reflectors demonstrated improved absorption compared to 1D designs, but with a substantial increase in thickness. To further optimize the absorption, the 2D reflectors were modified to incorporate a 3D photonic band gap in a more efficient design, resulting in the highest absorption and a more versatile reflector, applicable to a wide range of absorption spectra, including ultrathin films, making them more suitable for applications in ultrathin photovoltaic devices.

This paper introduces a novel approach called Credal Valuation Networks (CVNs) for addressing uncertain decision-making challenges. CVNs are unique in leveraging the credal sets framework to model uncertainty in attribute values within a decision-making scenario, distinguishing themselves from existing valuation networks by incorporating credal sets instead of probability distributions. We propose a two-stage method to optimize CVNs, incorporating a relaxation-based method to find an approximate solution within a convex set, and a precise solver to find the optimal solution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CVNs through a series of experiments across three applications: multi-objective optimization, path selection in probabilistic graphs, and group decision-making. Our results show that CVNs outperform current methods in precision and efficiency.

In recent years, Metric Learning-based methods have gained significant attention for Top-K recommendations, as they enable learning similarity measures that prioritize items similar to user historical preferences and discourage dissimilar items. However, these methods' reliance on pair-wise data mining and fixed margins limits their effectiveness. To address this, we introduce a novel Metric Learning approach called Probabilistic Metric Training with Adaptive Margin (PM-TAM), which eliminates the need for pair-wise data mining and introduces margins that dynamically adjust to user preferences. PM-TAM is built on Metric Learning with Probabilistic Margin (MLPM), a Metric Learning method that has previously been developed. By incorporating MLPM's probabilistic loss function and applying it to the Top-K recommendation task, PM-TAM achieves self-adaptive margins that prioritize the similarity between preferred and less-preferred items. Furthermore, our theoretical analysis reveals that PM-TAM can effectively optimize the probabilistic loss function, and our experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate its superiority over existing state-of-the-art methods.

The concept of non-Markovianity is a crucial aspect in understanding the dynamics of open quantum systems. Various definitions and detection methods have been proposed, yet it remains unclear whether all these definitions are interconnected. In this work, we demonstrate that several prominent definitions of non-Markovianity are interdependent, particularly within the framework of quantum channels. We provide a comprehensive analysis of these definitions, highlighting that some are capable of encompassing others. Furthermore, our investigation focuses on the concept of eternal non-Markovianity, which signifies the channels' non-Markovian behavior across all operational timescales. We discover that several previously proposed necessary conditions are insufficient for guaranteeing eternal non-Markovianity, while a specific condition is established as both necessary and sufficient for this property.

In high-stakes applications like medical diagnosis, decision-makers often lack sufficient training data and must rely on unlabelled real-world data to make informed choices. To address this issue, we propose a novel hybrid approach that integrates counterfactual reasoning with active learning to improve decision-making. Our method, which involves generating hypothetical scenarios to inform counterfactual reasoning, outperformed a comparable baseline on both synthetic and real-world datasets, achieving up to a 12.5% boost in accuracy. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of using counterfactual reasoning to select training instances for active learning, enhancing its effectiveness.

The field of autonomous robotics is rapidly evolving, with a significant emphasis on creating semantic maps that provide detailed, structured representations of an environment. This paper introduces a novel tool, RoSmEEry, designed to evaluate and improve the performance of semantic mapping algorithms. RoSmEEry generates large-scale, photo-realistic 3D scenes with embedded semantic information, which are then simulated in a real-time setting where a robotic platform navigates the environment, interacts with various objects, and collects data. This generated data is used to evaluate the accuracy of semantic mapping algorithms. To demonstrate the capabilities of RoSmEEry, we outline the development of a benchmark environment and present preliminary results on the performance of a state-of-the-art semantic mapping algorithm.

Rikudo is a tile-matching game derived from the Tetris concept, but it allows for flexible piece configurations. The Rikudo problem, which determines if a given input can be transformed into a predetermined high-score configuration, has been proven to be a complex, NP-complete issue. This proof, which is grounded in a reduction to the Multi-Dimensional Bin Packing problem, provides an NP-hardness foundation for Rikudo and its various special cases.

Optimal transport theory's increased popularity in machine learning and sciences is largely attributed to its ability to find efficient matching solutions. This is achieved through a cost function that measures distance between probability measures. However, a significant challenge in OT lies in its high computational complexity, making it difficult to apply to large-scale datasets. This complexity stems from the OT problem's dimensionality and the need for gradient computations, highlighting the need for specialized numerical techniques to address these issues. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive overview of OT's computational challenges and solutions.

Ramanujan identified integral modular equations that tie hypergeometric functions for positive integers, which for many cases has a connection to Hecke's congruences related to Euler's zeta function. This paper explores a novel approach to these identities, using Hecke's groups and representations theoretically tied to Ramanujan's modular identities, thereby shedding light on some of Ramanujan's pioneering ideas.

We have obtained high-resolution R~20,000 and R~40,000 VLT/UVES and Keck/Hires spectra of eight lensed quasars, each with a redshift of 1.7. Utilizing these spectra, we have determined the redshifts of 13 lensing galaxies within these systems, a key component of COSMOs. Our analysis revealed that the observed lensing galaxies are situated near the CMASS region, with their redshifts consistent with the previously determined values from VLT/UVES spectra. Our study also includes the detailed kinematics of the lensing systems, including the motion of the quasars relative to the deflectors, and a new measurement of the motion of the deflectors relative to the background quasars.

This paper introduces a novel approach for solving $q$-fractional differential equations on time scales. By transforming the equations into $q$-fractional integrals using a Volterra function, and then inverting this integration process, we establish two distinct integrals. We subsequently apply these inverted integrals in conjunction with the Volterra function to derive the solution forms for the $q$-fractional differential equations under specific initial conditions.

The emergence of a phonon Hall effect in one-dimensional vibrations within hexagonal materials like graphite is linked to a novel type of topological characteristic called the "Dirac index", which signifies the presence of a boundary between areas with distinct phonon band structures. This 'Dirac index' serves as the fundamental source of the phonon Hall effect and generates topological influences on the behavior of one-dimensional vibrations. Our research demonstrates that the topological shifts in phonon band structures can be identified through the application of a mathematical formula derived from the Bethe-Bloch theorem, enabling the prediction of phonon Hall effects within various materials.

A novel Raman imaging approach utilizes the Nod and Shuffle Integrated Circuit technology to capture a broad range of Raman information across 20 spectral regions. This method, which relies on a single laser excitation and multiple spectral collections, enhances data acquisition efficiency. By applying the technique to Raman imaging, researchers can significantly reduce acquisition times. Our approach involves two main steps: first, a single laser excitation is applied to the sample, and second, the sample is scanned across the NISC chip for multiple spectral collections. This enables the use of spectral analysis techniques, such as multivariate analysis, to extract Raman information from the collected data. Our method was successfully demonstrated through the imaging of a DNA mixture sample, which utilized the Nod and Shuffle Integrated Circuit technology to identify the two DNA components. Our approach was also validated by comparing the results with those obtained using traditional Raman imaging and multivariate analysis.

This article introduces matrix-based variations of Fejér and Levin-Ste\v{c}kin inequalities. Specifically, it establishes a matrix version of Fej\'{e}r's inequality under the condition that a sequence of matrices is semi-definite preserving and its sequence of singular values converges to a convergent sequence. Furthermore, the paper derives a matrix-based counterpart of Levin-Ste\v{c}kin's inequality under the condition that a sequence of matrices is contractive.

We investigate the mean null energy condition for an asymptotically anti-de Sitter black hole as it evolves and evaporates, drawing on the latest research in the causal evolution theory of the big bang and its implications for initial singularity and time of emergence. By applying this causal theory to an evaporating black hole, we can define a null hypersurface within its manifold and explore the properties of the mean null energy density along this hypersurface. Our findings indicate that this mean null energy density remains non-negative throughout the black hole's evolution, effectively confirming the strong energy condition for the early universe. Moreover, this strong energy condition holds until the point at which the black hole has evaporated, leaving open the possibility that the strong energy condition may be satisfied at the onset of the universe, contrary to conventional wisdom.

In this in-depth analysis, we demonstrate that conformal field theories (CFTs) with a specific symmetry group G can be represented as harmonic functions within the framework of Wigner's classification. By examining the dimensions of the theory in relation to the representations of G, we identify a significant number of theories with unique properties. These unique theories are characterized by having dimensions that are not equivalent to those found within the unitary series of G. Our study confirms the existence of 52 distinct theories, including $\mathcal{N}=1$ four-dimensional rank-2 gauge theories, $\mathcal{N}=2$ three-dimensional rank-1 and rank-2 gauge theories, four-dimensional free fermionic theories, five-dimensional free fermionic gauge theories, four-dimensional and five-dimensional theories with specific symmetries, as well as four-dimensional and five-dimensional free fermionic conformal field theories.

Significant advancements in industrial technologies and the digital transformation have led to increased interconnectedness among diverse systems, yielding substantial benefits but also introducing new vulnerabilities to cyber threats. Given the severity of these threats, it is essential to prioritize cybersecurity measures. This paper presents the Industrial Control System Cybersecurity Testing Maturity Model (ICS-CTM2), a new cybersecurity framework for testing control systems, aiming to provide a structured approach to evaluating an organization's cybersecurity capabilities. The model's development drew from existing cybersecurity frameworks, such as SANS 20 Critical Controls and ICS-SCP2, and incorporates feedback from experts in the field. ICS-CTM2 outlines a 15-point framework that delves into the core of cybersecurity testing, addressing aspects such as planning, risk management, and implementation, as well as compliance and documentation. The paper also discusses the practical applications of ICS-CTM2 and offers insights into its development process.

In a scenario involving cooperative Markov games, a specific problem is explored where a system manager coordinates n agents to reach an optimal state. The system manager has complete knowledge of the environment and can ensure the agents comply with their decisions. The primary goal is to find a policy that maximizes the total reward within a set time frame. A new approach called GWOR represents the overall system value based on individual actions, merging ideas from previous multi-objective methods with approaches that consider actions as vectors. The approach then uses a greedy-based algorithm to find the optimal policy. The results show that GWOR achieves better performance compared to established methods like GPD and MAML, especially in complex environments.

Pretrained language models have long been used in NLP tasks, but recent research has highlighted their role in perpetuating societal biases. This study focuses on an understudied area of bias – stereotypical bias – which refers to the tendency to hold preconceived notions about specific social groups. To investigate this, we introduce StereoSet, a new benchmark for assessing stereotypical bias in pretrained language models, specifically focusing on models trained from the English Web Text corpus. Our findings demonstrate that models trained on this corpus exhibit significant bias towards women and the LGBTQ+ community, with some bias being as strong as that found in non-pretrained models. Furthermore, we examine the impact of different bias mitigation techniques on stereotypical bias, revealing that some methods can have unintended consequences and confirm the importance of accounting for stereotypical bias in NLP tasks.

The increasing demand for clean energy and the need to reduce costs have driven the need for more efficient electrical tilt control of wind turbines. To address this challenge, we propose a novel off-policy reinforcement learning method that optimizes the tilt control of wind turbines at a distance. By utilizing real-time measurements and a low-fidelity model, our approach learns the optimal control strategy without the need for detailed physical simulations. The off-policy method ensures that the learned policy meets safety criteria, and we demonstrate its efficacy by applying it to the wind turbine domain. The results show that our method outperforms other advanced reinforcement learning algorithms by delivering significantly better performance, achieving up to a 20% improvement in power output.

A comprehensive update is presented on the value of the CP-violating phase $\gamma$, within the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix, based on a combination of LHCb's flavour-specific $B$ decays. The used data includes full 2011 and 2012 data sets, and a portion of the 2015 data set. The outcome is based on a combination of separate observations of $B^0$ and $B^0_s$ decays within three different categories: lepton plus hadrons, and a further division based on lepton flavor, and decays with b hadrons plus D decays. The outcome is of the following values, and uncertainties: $\gamma=(72.1^{+1.3}_{-2.0}({\rm stat.}) ^{+1.4}_{-1.3}({\rm syst.}) ^{+0.0}_{-0.3}({\rm PDG}) )^\circ$. The uncertainty is due to the following sources: data statistics, experimental methods and physical limitations.

This paper delves into the geometric properties of a specific family of ellipsoids in the context of hyperbolic space, where the family serves as an extension of traditional ellipsoids existing within Euclidean space. The study of these ellipsoids becomes particularly engaging when the family exhibits a non-trivial automorphism group resulting from complex symmetries. The research focuses on two distinct types of complex symmetries, referred to as type I and type II, which have implications for the family's automorphism groups. Type I, which can be understood as a combination of reflections, yields an infinite number of distinct, non-congruent ellipsoids. In contrast, type II, which arises from rotations, results in a finite number of unique ellipsoids. The study further explores the geometric characteristics of these ellipsoids, including their invariants and the manner in which they intersect with hyperbolic planes. The research also examines the possibility of degenerate cases where the ellipsoids degenerate into planes or lines.

A significant shift in the data landscape is underway as the General Data Protection Regulation comes into effect, allowing individuals to buy, sell, and trade their personal data on emerging platforms. The question remains as to how individuals will respond to these new market opportunities. In our study, we examine how people perceive and engage with personal data transactions, specifically whether receiving data-based benefits can motivate them to sell their data, and whether they are willing to disclose sensitive information in exchange for compensation. Through a large-scale online experiment involving 1,014 participants, we found that individuals value data protection and are cautious when sharing their data, yet still willing to sell personal data for financial benefits. However, we also found that the type of data shared and the purpose for which it is used influence these decisions, with individuals being more cautious when sharing sensitive information in low-trust environments. The outcomes of this study provide insights into designing personal data markets that are both economically efficient and socially responsible.

In 5G and beyond 5G networks, Quicker-than-Nyquist (QTN) signaling is a critical technique used to increase system spectral efficiency. However, detecting QTN signaling poses a significant challenge for traditional receivers due to the significant increase in channel distortion. This study proposes a novel approach to address the issue by combining deep learning with list sphere decoding to detect QTN signaling. To optimize the algorithm's performance, a training method is developed that incorporates knowledge about the original QTN transmission and standard Nyquist signaling. The algorithm is then tested using both static and Rayleigh-fading channels under various QTN and SNR conditions. Results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms traditional receivers, with a reduction of up to 2 dB in required SNR for 10% and 5% bit error rates for standard QTN patterns.

We explore the order topology and Frink ideal structure of effect algebras with Archimedean components, focusing on effect algebras that are not necessarily unital. Our research yields four criteria for determining when a non-unital effect algebra is topologically equivalent to a unital effect algebra. We derive a significant implication: for non-unital c*-effect algebras, order topology determines rational inner order if and only if the c*-norm is continuous. Additionally, we establish a condition for c*-effect alges to be Riesz effect spaces: they are either unital Riesz effect spaces or non-unital with a central abundant *-subgroup. We also show that a non-unital full effect algebra is Riesz if and only if it is Riesz for its unitification. Furthermore, we provide a necessary and sufficient condition for a non-unital effect algebra to be Riesz and provide a characterization of Riesz type for c*-effect algebras. We also explore the order topology and Frink ideal structure of non-unital c*-effect algebras and establish a condition for non-unital c*-effect alges to be Riesz.

Recent advancements in deep learning models have achieved exceptional performance across various applications. Nevertheless, these models often rely on extensive, highly structured, and expensive data sets to reach their top performance. In response, data augmentation has emerged as a crucial technique to mitigate the expense of labeling data. Although data augmentation has been utilized for a considerable period, the primary focus has been on the type of transformation and its impact on the entire image, rather than the specific features of interest. In this study, we introduce a data augmentation strategy that targets and blends the salient object segments within an image. This allows the model to concentrate on multiple objects of interest, enhancing object diversity within a data set. Furthermore, the model learns to recognize objects that may not be typical examples of their class. Experimental evaluations across object detection and image classification demonstrate that our proposed approach yields enhanced performance.

Consider the group $G = \mathrm{GL}_\infty(\mathbb{Z}_p)$. The associated Iwahori--Hecke algebra, $A$, can be viewed as an algebra of functions on $G$. We will focus on a specific set of linear functionals, referred to as $\mathcal{G}$, on this algebra, which extend to continuous linear functions on the inductive limit of $A$. We propose that these functionals are equivalent to $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$-twists of characters of $L_p(\mathbb{Z})$. We prove that this holds for a subset of $\mathcal{G}$ with a specific property under the assumption of a key conjecture. We also explore the relationship between $\mathcal{G}$ and representations of $A$ and find that these functionals are connected to such representations. We establish that any representation of $A$ with a non-zero trace has a specific property. We also demonstrate that any representation of $A$ with a trace in $\mathcal{G}$ has a unique factorization of a specific type. We further examine the relationship between the trace of a representation and the associated $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$-twist of a character of $L_p(\mathbb{Z})$ and show that they are linked by a specific property. A new, flexible gravitational theory known as Horndeski theory is examined to determine its potential to alter the fundamental cosmic principles. By studying how the theory's most common variations impact the cosmic pattern, it's possible to establish a framework for testing its validity. A novel method for analyzing the cosmic pattern using a combination of data from galaxy alignments within individual galaxies and the large-scale light emitted by galaxies is developed. The approach is designed to be independent of the assumptions made in standard cosmological models and can be used to test the validity of the gravitational theory by analyzing the patterns of light and the relationships between galaxies. The research also explores the potential for using this method to constrain the parameters of the gravitational theory by simulating the patterns of light emitted by galaxies and the relationships between galaxies using a variety of gravitational models, and then comparing these simulated results to the patterns of light and the relationships between galaxies as observed in the data. The research finds that the patterns of light emitted by galaxies and the relationships between galaxies provide a powerful tool for testing the validity of the gravitational theory, and that the patterns of light emitted by galaxies are particularly sensitive to the parameters of the gravitational theory, making them useful for constraining the parameters of the theory. The research also shows that the relationships between galaxies are less sensitive to the parameters of the gravitational theory, but that combining the patterns of light emitted by galaxies with the relationships between galaxies can provide a more comprehensive understanding of the gravitational theory.

In the field of soft matter physics, the study of non-equilibrium rheology has gained significant attention. Our research involves investigating the effects of external forces on the dynamics of soft particles with variable sizes and repulsive interactions. We examine the behavior of these particles under the influence of a constant force and a force that oscillates in magnitude. Our results show that particles can exhibit high elasticity, even at low concentrations, which increases as the force strength increases. We also observe that certain types of oscillating forces can induce a non-linear, universal response in the particles, characterized by a high elasticity, even at low concentrations. Furthermore, we identify a specific condition under which particles behave in a non-linear, low-frequency manner, exhibiting a high elasticity, even at low concentrations.

A novel computational approach is presented, combining classical molecular dynamics simulations with machine learning to quantify the gold melting point across various particle sizes and temperatures. Evaluating the accuracy of this method against established and newly derived reference melting points, particularly for a 3 nanometer and 1 micrometer particle, it is demonstrated that small 100 atom gold nanoparticles exhibit a higher melting point compared to larger 100,000 atom particles. However, using machine learning to correct for the system size effect enables accurate melting point predictions for particles in the 1-100 nanometer range.

This is the beginning of a series focused on the creation and proof of
generalized theorems concerning the breakdown points of a particular mathematical
operator, known as the $(-\Delta^{(2)}_0)$-Laplacian, within the space of
functions with bounded variation, denoted by $\BV(\R^N)$. The goal of this paper
is to outline a general approach for proving such theorems, which can be adapted
to various types of differential operators. This paper lays the groundwork by
introducing a novel parameterized splitting theorem, which is a more versatile
version of the well-known PDE splitting theorem, along with a parameterized
bifurcation result. This result is then applied to a specific case involving the
$(-\Delta^{(2)}_0)$-Laplacian.

The concept of taste is a complex, yet incomplete aspect of human perception, with four established tastes - sweet, sour, bitter, and salty - but a long-standing debate exists over whether there is a fifth taste, "umami." Recent research supports the incorporation of umami as a distinct taste, and our analysis, utilizing taste profiles from 200 subjects, validates this notion, further highlighting the inherent asymmetry in human taste perceptions.
We derive new identities for (h, q)-Genocchi numbers and polynomials using the Beta function.

In clinical settings, researchers often seek to predict how patients will respond to future treatments, but existing methods are limited by their inability to account for long-term effects of interventions. To address this, we propose a novel approach using reinforcement learning to estimate the cumulative impact of treatments on outcomes over time. Our method can be applied in situations where only the final outcome is observed, such as in medical billing systems. We demonstrate its effectiveness through a simulation study and prove the robustness of its results, which are also interpretable in terms of expected future rewards.

In case-control studies, participants are selected based on the presence of an outcome and often face recall biases that can skew the association between a predictor and the outcome. These biases are usually overlooked in the analysis, which can result in biased findings. To address this issue, we suggest a method that incorporates recall biases into the analysis, allowing for a more accurate assessment of the relationship between a predictor and the outcome. This method involves modeling the distribution of the predictor among controls and participants, and then using these models to estimate the causal effect of the predictor on the outcome. This approach can be applied to both continuous and binary predictors, and can be used with varying levels of information about the recall process. When applied to a dataset of patients with sepsis, our analysis revealed that pre-existing mobility issues had a significant impact on the development of the condition.

Generative models can be divided into two components: a data encoder that transforms input data into latent space and a generative unit that transforms these latent values into a form that can be understood. Traditionally, the encoder is a linear process, while the generator is a neural network. This separation allows for the use of closed-form training for linear encoders and maximum likelihood training for the generator. However, the linear encoding process has limitations, such as poor performance in complex data and limited scalability. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces a new method for training generative models using reversible layers, which can be considered as a combination of closed-form encoding and autoregressive generative units. This new method is an efficient alternative to traditional generative models, such as VAEs and GANs, and can be easily applied to various generative models, including those with multiple data distributions.

The concept of smart cities has gained significant attention in recent years, focusing on enhancing the quality of life for its citizens while fostering sustainable development. Effective urban planning and management require a substantial amount of reliable and up-to-date data on various urban characteristics, which can be collected from public sources and attributed to specific geographical locations. This study presents an innovative data analysis method that identifies interrelated patterns in spatially referenced data sets. By applying this method, we can generate different types of visualizations that reveal the attributes associated with these patterns. Experimental results demonstrate the method's capabilities, and we demonstrate its applicability by analyzing real-world data from the city of Vienna.

This work explores the HDG-P0 methods for reaction-diffusion and Stokes equations, focusing on developing optimal geometric multigrid preconditioners. To achieve this, we employ the HDG coercivity theory and establish local matrix conditioning using the maximum norm. Building upon this, we create an hypervolume norm-based matrix norm and demonstrate that the multigrid preconditioner is nearly optimal. To further investigate, we develop an HDG-P0 method with a novel finite element space for reaction-diffusion equations, which maintains the established optimal preconditioner. To validate our theoretical findings, we perform extensive numerical experiments and confirm the accuracy of our predictions.

A widely used data analysis method called sensitivity assessment aims to understand how missing data affect the reliability of findings, but this process is often complex and time-consuming. In this study, we developed a new Bayesian framework that can efficiently quantify the risk of false discoveries in the presence of missing data, also evaluating the impact of missing covariates on this risk. By leveraging the E-value, a recently introduced metric for quantifying evidence reliability, our approach can provide a nuanced understanding of the implications of missing data, taking into account the relationship between missing and observed data. In a simulated study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of our method by comparing it to a traditional frequentist approach and showed that our approach can accurately estimate the impact of missing data on the reliability of findings, also reducing computational costs. In real-world data from the Women's Health Initiative, our method revealed significant challenges in assessing the reliability of findings, highlighting the importance of considering the relationship between missing and observed data in sensitivity assessments.

In crossover trials where multiple treatment periods are employed to assess treatment effects, subjects who drop out prematurely can lead to missing data, compromising the trial's validity and potentially producing biased estimates of treatment impact. Several approaches have been proposed to handle missing data in crossover trials, including the use of multiple imputation, joint modeling, and single imputation techniques. However, these methods often require specific assumptions about the data distribution, which may not be easily met. To address this limitation, a new method for missing data analysis in crossover trials based on probability is introduced. This approach involves estimating treatment effects by comparing the probabilities of achieving specific outcomes between treatment periods, allowing for more accurate and less restrictive assumptions about the data distribution. Furthermore, this method enables the analysis of treatment effects at specific time points, without requiring specific assumptions about the data distribution. Its efficacy has been demonstrated through simulation studies, and an analysis of a real-world clinical trial has been provided to illustrate its application.

We define and explore the concepts of weakly monoidal frameworks and monoidal frameworks on categories.  A weakly monoidal framework can be viewed as a category equipped with a specific structure that includes a collection of data elements, representing various compositions, associators, and other components necessary for a robust framework.  A monoidal framework is an extension of this concept where these components meet specific coherence criteria, enabling the framework to function coherently.  By examining the properties of these frameworks, we demonstrate their existence and provide an example in the context of simplicial complexes, specifically the Stasheff A(n) complexes, whose associahedra form a sequence of simplicial frameworks that meet the coherence criteria, resulting in a monoidal framework.

As memory becomes an increasingly significant performance bottleneck in modern systems, integrating logic within memory to improve performance, energy efficiency, and bandwidth has become essential. However, current memory controllers lack the flexibility to accommodate various logic circuits, which hinders the potential of logic-in-memory. To address this limitation, we propose the CODIC system, which consists of a CODIC core, memory controller, and internal communication system. The CODIC core, embedded within the memory controller, provides a low-cost solution for enabling logic-in-memory. The core is complemented by an optimization framework that allows users to create custom logic-in-memory programs. The CODIC system is validated through simulations and real-world testing, demonstrating its ability to achieve significant performance improvements in various memory applications.

This paper is the second in a series that showcases how functional programming promotes efficient management and coordination of virtualized network resources. Focusing on its impact on network evolution and design, we delve into the role of monads in enabling networks to evolve incrementally. By applying the Resource Monads Approach, we outline a design methodology that captures a network's evolution in code, leveraging monadic types to document resource assumptions, and confining their scope to necessary areas. Key design principles are also discussed to facilitate smooth network changes.

To develop practical quantum error correction, it's essential to understand how to enhance the speed of logical gate operations in quantum codes. We investigate this issue by comparing the efficiency of logical gates in the toric code, focusing on the relationship between single and multiple qubits. We found that single-qubit operations on a toric code's surface can be executed at a rate of $10^8$ Hz, whereas multi-qubit operations require at least $10^2$ times more time, resulting in a rate of $10^9$ Hz. We also identified that the toric code's surface can be treated as a unitary filter for entanglement, with single-qubit operations creating multi-partite entanglement that can be stabilized through local measurements. However, this process is hindered by decoherence, particularly when the distance of the toric code is small. We determined that the rate of logical operations is significantly affected by the time required to stabilize the entanglement, resulting in a rate that is $10^2$ times slower than the ideal rate.

The VO standards initiative aims to simplify access to diverse observatory assets, fostering a unified, interoperable environment for enabling task-oriented applications. The VO standards provide a standardized approach for controlling remote instruments and observing platforms, enabling seamless data discovery, retrieval, and integration. We present a task-oriented control system, OPUS, designed to execute complex workflows with enhanced efficiency and flexibility. OPUS leverages the VO standards, specifically the Observation Core Protocol (OCP) API, to communicate with remote instruments, allowing for the execution of sophisticated tasks that can adapt to various configurations, models, and data formats. OPUS is adaptable to new assets as they become available, facilitating the rapid development of complex applications and workflows, and promoting innovation through prototyping and process optimization.

This research proposes a novel approach to teaching network management techniques through interactive simulations. Digital game-based learning has gained acceptance in education, and our study builds upon this concept by developing a digital game to model and simulate complex wireless networks. The game allows players to create and manage networks, with built-in algorithms facilitating game interactions and evaluation of player performance. By leveraging digital game-based learning, this game-based approach has been shown to be more engaging and effective in understanding network concepts than traditional teaching methods.

The relationship between ozone and oxygen concentrations in Earth-like atmospheres, crucial for understanding and modeling planetary conditions, is often taken for granted but is explored further in this study. The concentration of molecular oxygen in Earth's atmosphere has been calculated using a simplified model of atmospheric chemistry and boundary conditions, showing a range of possible values based on ozone concentration and atmospheric conditions. The results indicate that the ozone-to-oxygen ratio can be influenced by atmospheric oxygen levels, particularly at high and low extremes, suggesting that the concentration of ozone is not solely determined by terrestrial atmospheric conditions. Additionally, the concentration of ozone in Earth's atmosphere has been found to be dependent on the scale height of the planet, particularly at high altitudes. The findings of this study have implications for modeling and interpreting planetary atmospheres, particularly those of exoplanets.

The Hofstadter butterfly model has been expanded to include higher dimensions, where Hofstadter bands exhibit a complex, fractal energy spectrum influenced by both magnetic flux and spatial boundary conditions. This results in a topological structure that is fundamentally three-dimensional in nature, with the creation of Chern invariants along its edges. This work explores the Hofstadter model in three dimensions, focusing on the energy surface of Chern states in the presence of a magnetic flux, with the observation of persistent surface currents. This phenomenon is robust against both energy fluctuations and spatial disorder, with the surface currents even resisting the introduction of edge states caused by periodic boundary conditions.

Multilingual pre-trained models have shown remarkable language representation capabilities across various domains, but often struggle when applied to specialized fields such as medicine. To enhance their performance within specific domains, we propose a simple yet effective post-training adjustment technique that utilizes domain-specific data to improve results. This approach is particularly beneficial when the available domain-specific data is limited, and therefore, we had to curtail the model's size to prevent overfitting. We evaluated our method on an Italian medical corpus, comparing it to a model trained solely on English data. The results indicate that our approach not only outperforms the model without domain adjustment but also surpasses the performance of a model with unlimited resources when given limited medical resources.

A new theoretical investigation explores the formation of altered-ion-acoustic waves, specifically solitary and shock waves, in a plasma system consisting of hot electrons, warm ions, and superimposed positively charged dust grains. The study examines how different parameters such as dust grain charge, ion fluid temperature, and electron nonthermal velocity, influence wave properties such as speed, amplitude, and compression, using both analytical and numerical methods. The results show that wave properties can be controlled by adjusting the values of these parameters. The inclusion of warm ions and negatively charged dust grains causes a significant increase in wave speed, while the addition of positively charged dust grains reduces the speed and changes the wave type from shock to solitary waves. The study also reveals that dust grains can increase the speed of altered-ion-acoustic waves, while the presence of ion fluid temperature and nonthermal electrons can reduce it. The study demonstrates that the inclusion of dust grains can change the wave properties, such as changing a shock wave into a solitary wave, and also changes the wave's compression. The results of this study are applicable to various astrophysical and space plasma systems.

This study introduces an unsupervised pretraining method for multi-lingual sentence representation, which utilizes cross-lingual context information to create compact representations. By applying multi-lingual encoder-decoder alignment and translating between sentences in different languages, the proposed approach generates cross-lingual context-aware embeddings. These cross-lingual context-aware embeddings are then used to pretrain a multi-lingual sentence model that can effectively capture context-specific information across languages. Experimental results on public benchmarks for English and non-English languages demonstrate that the pretrained model outperforms existing systems, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

Multimodal learning models have achieved significant success in handling diverse modalities, yet their performance is often hindered by the presence of noisy or redundant information. To address this issue, we present an efficient and adaptable framework called Prototypical Modal Adjustment (PMR), capable of selectively processing relevant modalities for specific tasks. By identifying and representing distinct concept types in a shared semantic space, our framework can identify the most useful modalities for each concept, thereby enhancing overall performance. To demonstrate the effectiveness of PMR, we conducted a series of experiments on the public Multimodal Emotion Recognition in the Wild (EMO) dataset, achieving a notable accuracy of 68.11%, which surpasses the state-of-the-art results.

We examine the transport behavior of color charges within the context of an expanding plasma, where the electromagnetic fields' influence is maximized through their interaction with the charges' color charges. This interaction leads to the emergence of new sources within the Fokker-Planck and Boltzmann equations, previously absent in equations based solely on charge charges. This effect is quantifiable and can be incorporated into existing simulations of the Fokker-Planck and Boltzmann equations. Notably, our analysis reveals that under certain conditions, the impact of the electromagnetic fields' influence on the charges can be substantial, even reaching a 50% engagement with the charges.

This study presents a novel approach to enhancing spoken command recognition through the application of deep neural networks. By leveraging a hybrid model that combines a deep neural network's initial classification layer with a tensor-train network for feature extraction, our method has demonstrated superior performance. In particular, the proposed hybrid model outperformed traditional CNN and TDNN models in evaluation, achieving a significant 10.7% improvement in spurious activation suppression and 7.0% improvement in overall accuracy in the CMU Mirme and 2s-AGZ datasets. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the hybrid model can effectively reduce computational complexity while maintaining comparable performance to its fully-computed counterpart.

The non-Markovian dynamics of open quantum systems is analyzed using two distinct master equation formats: the Lindbladian representation and the collapse-dissipative model. Both approaches yield equivalent dynamics for the system-Environment state, with the Lindbladian representation adhering to a semi-group property. We develop a method to generate non-Markovian quantum jump trajectories based on the Lindbladian master equation and compare it to the trajectories derived from the collapse-dissipative model. This comparison facilitates an investigation of the impact of the initial state on the behavior of quantum-jump trajectories.

The integration of plasmonic nanoparticles with thin-film silicon solar cells has been identified as a promising method to boost their absorption capabilities. A comprehensive investigation into the effect of varying the dimensions and forms of aluminum nanoparticles on the performance of silicon solar cells has been conducted. By employing a rigorous numerical approach, specifically the finite-difference time-domain method, we have examined the influence of different shapes on the solar cells' absorption properties. Our study revealed that both the size and form of the nanoparticles have a substantial impact on the solar cells' ability to capture light, with a 2.5% increase in absorption observed when compared to unmodified cells. A thorough analysis of the solar cells' absorption spectra and the nanoparticles' plasmon resonances provided valuable insights into the underlying mechanisms driving light absorption.

The concept of datalog is based on a logic program language that uses facts and rules to derive conclusions. It is known for its efficient processing capabilities, being capable of handling queries in polynomial time within tree-shaped data structures. However, its application to complex graphs reveals a significant challenge, as datalog is insufficient to solve certain PTIME problems. To address this limitation, a new language, called datalog+, has been developed by introducing a set operator called choice. Datalog+ extends its capabilities by allowing the selection of at most one rule from a set. Interestingly, by incorporating this set operator, datalog+ can express all PTIME problems, but it falls short of expressing the entire NP-complete class.

Deep learning has become increasingly popular in various fields such as image and video processing, natural language processing, and drug design, due to its ability to achieve high accuracy. However, its high power and memory requirements have hindered its practical applications. To overcome this challenge, a novel co-design approach is proposed, which integrates algorithmic and hardware enhancements to create an energy-efficient long short-term memory neural network. This co-design approach leverages hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition to compress the neural network, which results in significant reductions in parameters and a substantial decrease in power consumption. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves a 95.7% power reduction and 1.5% accuracy loss for video identification, and it is scalable to large-scale applications.

The MAVLink protocol, used by MAVLink-compliant systems such as drones and ground stations, is susceptible to attacks due to its vulnerability, a problem that affects systems like Ardupilot and PX4. These vulnerabilities can be exploited by hackers to gain control over UAVs. To address this issue, we developed MAVSec, a security framework that protects MAVLink communications and enhances the protocol's security. MAVSec includes a secure MAVLink proxy that filters and signs messages, a TLS server, and a secure client. MAVSec also integrates with the Linux kernel to create a secure network interface, ensuring that only authorized packets are transmitted. By using MAVSec, users can secure their UAVs and protect them from attacks, a feature that we demonstrated by implementing and testing MAVSec on a small drone. Our results show that MAVSec can prevent unauthorized access and control of UAVs, a capability that is essential for preventing malicious actions.

We introduce a straightforward framework for creating a virtualized network structure on a dynamic group of computers with unpredictable membership. Our framework, named Kollaps, can replicate various network types, including those with multiple sub-networks, custom packet routing, or virtualized devices. Kollaps achieves correct packet forwarding in complex scenarios by utilizing a centralised routing table and per-host queues, ensuring that packets are delivered in the correct order. In networks with distinct sub-networks, packets may be temporarily routed between these sub-networks, necessitating a novel algorithm to ensure packet ordering across changing network connections. Kollaps's design is verified through simulation, validated on small-scale networks, and demonstrated on a dynamic, large-scale network with over 1,000 computers.

The exact mathematical link between the Newman-Penrose (NP) Weyl tensor decomposition in complex space and the underlying geometry in twistor space remains unclear. The NP decomposition itself doesn't naturally fit within Penrose's original conformal twistor space framework. The problem is resolved by translating the NP decomposition into an equivalent form known as the self-dual twistor form. The resulting relationship between Weyl tensor components and twistor space structures, dubbed the Newman-Penrose map, is non-linear and highly singular. The goal of this paper is to explore the behavior of this singular map in specific scenarios, including its effects on null geodesics, its influence on complex projective transformations, and its relationship with complex conformal symmetries.

We've developed a lightweight, compact muon detector for underground mapping using cosmic rays. This detector employs a telescope-like setup of two scintillator bars to pinpoint muons originating from the Antarctic sky, allowing for the creation of detailed underground relief maps without compromising the Antarctic ice sheet.

This paper proposes a new format called LLP, a Parsing Expression derivative, 
capable of parsing either from left to right or right to left depending on 
circumstances. It's designed specifically for parsing languages like 
Lua, which has expression parsing requirements. 
We also introduce a related Parsing Expression, PE LLP, which can handle 
parsing tasks in both left-to-right and left-to-right directions. 
We also discuss the potential for further development.

This research explores the phenomenon of vacuum Cherenkov radiation within the context of a gauge theory that occurs when a charged particle with kinetic energy surpasses the mass difference between two different vacuum states of the theory. Building upon previous research, our study extends this idea to incorporate temperature effects. Specifically, we consider two scenarios: one in which the theory's gauge field decouples at a finite temperature, and another where it remains interacting. The initial scenario is analogous to a situation where the theory's gauge field is decoupled at absolute zero, allowing us to directly compare the results. In the second scenario, our analysis focuses on a simplified model of the theory, enabling us to demonstrate that a particle with sufficient energy can emit radiation even at high temperatures, with the rate of emission exhibiting a temperature dependence.

To predict how language will change over time, researchers must combine insights from historical language patterns and in-depth studies of speakers' thoughts and behaviors. A key question in the field is how people's language forecasts adapt in response to changes in the language environment. To address this, this study uses a unique dataset consisting of 18 million words from the Open American Corpus, a vast resource of spoken language. By leveraging this dataset and employing cutting-edge neural language models, the researchers made two significant discoveries. Firstly, they found that speakers' language forecasts are highly accurate, especially in predicting changes to their own daily conversations. Secondly, when speakers are exposed to changes in the language they interact with, their forecasts rapidly adjust within a short period, typically a few weeks or months. These findings highlight the value of using large-scale language models to study how people's language forecasts evolve in response to changing environments.

We introduce a straightforward yet powerful approach for learning the three-dimensional pose of objects directly from images by observing them as they rotate. Our proposed method, called "Turntables", relies on a standard convolutional neural network to predict the three-dimensional pose from a single image, without requiring any prior knowledge of the object's geometry. Observing objects as they turn allows us to derive additional geometric information, making it easier to determine their three-dimensional pose. To achieve this, we train the network to recognize when an object is being rotated, and use this information to calculate its three-dimensional pose. To evaluate our method, we created a comprehensive dataset of objects in different poses, and demonstrate that it outperforms existing approaches by a significant margin in determining three-dimensional pose from a single image, without needing any prior knowledge of object geometry.

In Andreev quantum dots, bound states significantly impact the transport characteristics when the bound state energy is aligned with the Fermi level. The crossed Andreev tunneling effect, which involves Andreev bound states, is particularly significant in multi-terminal semiconductor-superconductor nanowire and quantum dot devices. This study examines the transport properties of a two-terminal semiconductor quantum dot device with a superconductor nanowire incorporating a phase-biased superconducting electrode. The results show that the transport characteristics are influenced by the energy of the Andreev bound states, and the appearance of a discrete energy peak in the transport characteristics is associated with the formation of a bound state in the quantum dot. The peak in the transport characteristics can be adjusted by controlling the gate voltage, and the appearance of a negative differential conductance is linked to the formation of a bound state in the quantum dot. The study also examines the transport characteristics of a two-terminal semiconductor nanowire device with a phase-biased superconducting electrode. The results show that the transport characteristics are influenced by the formation of a bound state in the quantum dot, and the appearance of a negative differential conductance is associated with the formation of a bound state in the quantum dot.

To investigate the effects of an anisotropic velocity distribution on the acceleration of particles during magnetic reconnection in a hot plasma, a simulation is conducted using the Vlasov model, where magnetic turbulence scatters particles in a direction-dependent manner. The simulation reveals that anisotropic scattering significantly accelerates particles, causing a peak in the particle energy distribution to emerge rapidly due to magnetic reconnection. The anisotropic scattering effect leads to a substantial increase in the highest energy particles, causing them to rise rapidly as a sharp peak appears in the distribution. The peak in the distribution is found to be composed of two distinct populations: one that is accelerated by the magnetic reconnection process and another that is a result of anisotropic scattering. The accelerated particles are predominantly in the lower-energy tail of the distribution, whereas the anisotropic scattering causes the high-energy tail to rise rapidly. The anisotropic scattering is found to be a key factor in the rapid acceleration of particles, causing a sharp peak in the distribution.

We investigate the possibility of new, previously undiscovered Higgs bosons arising from the interactions of standard model fields. These new bosons can be combinations of the standard model Higgs boson, or other types such as the charged component of a new U(1)' gauge boson, or a combination of the standard model Higgs boson and a new, singlet scalar field. The interactions of these new bosons with standard model fields can be studied in experiments by examining the decay of the standard model Higgs boson into pairs of photons. The probability of this decay is influenced by the relative weights of the terms describing the interactions of the standard model Higgs boson with its components. The decay probability is also affected by the relative weights of the terms describing the interactions of the standard model Higgs boson with its components. The decay probability is sensitive to the relative weights of the terms describing the interactions of the standard model Higgs boson with its components. The sensitivity of the decay probability to the relative weights of the terms describing the interactions of the standard model Higgs boson with its components can be used to constrain the relative weights of the terms describing the interactions of the standard model Higgs boson with its components.
